LEDE: Achievement Distillation (Moon et al., NeurIPS 2023) is the strongest published model-free agent on Crafter. We trained it and its PPO baseline for the standard 1M environment steps, first on a Windows laptop with a 4 GB RTX 3050 and later on a Linux laptop with an RTX 5090, then added one change of our own: extra reward for achievements the agent rarely gets. Over three seeds it lifts PPO from 15.8 to 21.0. On Achievement Distillation it reaches 23.7 ± 1.1 over three seeds, against 17.7 for our single plain-AD seed and the paper's 21.8. Later sections ask why no agent reaches a diamond: every agent dies early, mostly to zombies at night or with an empty vital. They then test follow-ups aimed at that: a longer horizon, a GRU memory and a survival signal. Only the survival signal without a per-step cost makes the agent live longer. The last sections build our own world model of Crafter and let the agent practise in short dreams from it: that reaches iron twice as often and scores 26.1 ± 0.8, but the world model was trained on other agents' play, so this number is a diagnostic, not a benchmark result.
RESULT_TEXT: The charts and tree below compare the seed-0 runs. Seed 0 is a weak seed for the baselines: PPO scores 12.4 there, against 16.7 and 18.2 on seeds 1 and 2, and AD scores 17.7 against the paper's 21.8. Both baselines get stuck at the stone pickaxe on this seed, which locks them out of iron. The rarity bonus breaks that wall: with AD and β = 2, stone pickaxes go from 1.6% of episodes to 25%, iron from 0.2% to 5.6%, and defeated skeletons from 15% to 23%. The next table shows how much of the gain holds across seeds.
FINDINGS:
180 → 1,620 steps/s

World generation was the bottleneck

Resetting Crafter took about a second, because world generation calls a pure-Python noise function 82,000 times. Early episodes last ~170 steps and the 8 environments step in lockstep, so resets stalled everything. Installing numba, which the noise library uses automatically, cut a reset to 50 ms. The generated maps are bit-identical.

4.3 GB → 2.2 GB

The paper's batch does not fit in 4 GB

A 512-sample minibatch needs 4.3 GB in fp32. Windows then pages GPU memory to system RAM instead of failing, and training runs 15× slower. Each minibatch is now split into two halves whose gradients are summed, which gives the same update.

934 s → ~600 s

The distillation phase repeated work

Every 8 rollouts AD trains 6 epochs on its contrastive losses. The official loop re-runs the frozen old policy on every sample in every epoch, encodes the same goal frames once per time step, and makes 16 tiny GPU calls per trajectory. Doing each once gives the same losses and gradients (relative difference 2.7e-5 in exact fp32) and is 1.7× faster.

85% VRAM cap

Silent memory paging

The first fast version was slower than the original. Memory cached from the PPO phase plus the aux phase's varied batch shapes pushed past 4 GB, and Windows paged the excess. Capping PyTorch at 85% of VRAM and clearing its cache before the aux phase fixed it.

same seed, different game

Crafter is not bit-reproducible

Creatures are stored in Python sets ordered by memory address, and the game picks which zombie to despawn from that order. A fixed seed therefore diverges between processes after a few dozen steps. The rules are unaffected, but step-by-step comparisons between runs are not meaningful.
IMPROVE_TEXT:
The Crafter score is a geometric mean, so achievements stuck near 0% cost the most. When an achievement is unlocked for the first time in an episode, we add β · (1 − p) to the reward, where p is the share of the last 200 episodes that unlocked it. With β = 2, a common achievement keeps roughly its +1 and one the agent has never managed is worth +3. The score is still computed from the unmodified game. It is about 30 lines (RarityBonus in train.py, flag --rarity_bonus).

We wrote the prediction down before the first run: stone pickaxe, iron and eat plant would rise above zero. The first two did, in every configuration. Iron tools stayed rare: a handful of episodes in the bonus runs, and one of each in one plain-PPO seed. Eat plant stayed near zero (a few episodes per run at most) and diamonds at zero: eating a plant means planting a sapling and coming back hundreds of steps later, which a bonus cannot teach if the agent never does it once. The price is sleep: waking up drops from about 88% to 70% of episodes, because the agent spends that time on the tech tree.

  • PPO, 3 seeds: 15.75 → 18.58 (β = 1) → 20.99 (β = 2) → 20.14 (β = 4). About 1.3 hours per run.
  • Achievement Distillation, seed 0: 17.71 → 22.80 (β = 1) → 23.08 (β = 2). About 7 hours per run.
  • With AD, β = 2 starts slower than β = 1. It trails until about 600k steps, then overtakes it once the stone pickaxe takes off (63% of recent episodes at 780k steps, against 51%).

Seed 0 is unusually bad for the baselines, so the AD gain on that seed is probably larger than typical. The cleanest evidence is the three-seed PPO sweep. Seeds 1 and 2 of AD + rarity β = 2 were trained later on the RTX 5090 laptop with the same settings and scored 24.87 and 23.01. So the three-seed mean is 23.65 ± 1.05, above the paper's Achievement Distillation (21.79 ± 1.37 over 10 seeds). Plain AD and AD + rarity β = 1 still have one seed each.
REPRO:
# Windows, from the repo root (game sources and .venv are recreated by the setup script)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts/setup_windows.ps1

# Achievement Distillation, paper config, 1M steps (~7 h on an RTX 3050 Laptop)
.venv/Scripts/python methods/05_achievement_distillation/train.py --config ppo_ad --seed 0 --micro_batch 256 --aux_micro_batch 128

# PPO and PPO + rarity bonus, seeds 0-2, back to back (~1.3 h per run)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts/queue.ps1 -Config ppo -Bonus 0 -Prefix ppo -Seeds 0,1,2
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts/queue.ps1 -Config ppo -Bonus 2.0 -Prefix ppo-rarity2 -Seeds 0,1,2

# live dashboard (http://localhost:8765) and periodic checkpoint videos

SEEDS_TEXT: The three PPO seeds average 15.75, almost exactly the paper's 15.60, so the setup reproduces the published baseline. The bonus helps in proportion to its strength up to β = 2 and then levels off. At β = 1 the gain is uneven: +7.9, +1.7 and −1.1 seed by seed, large when the baseline gets stuck before the stone pickaxe and gone when it finds the pickaxe on its own. At β = 2 it is +8.4, +3.5 and +3.7, so every seed improves. The mean rises to 20.99 and the spread between seeds shrinks from 3.0 to 0.9. At β = 4 the mean drops slightly, to 20.14. Three seeds per arm is still a small sample (paired t = 3.3 for β = 2). AD + rarity β = 2 now has three seeds; seeds 1 and 2 were trained on the RTX 5090 laptop with the same settings as seed 0. It scores 23.65 ± 1.05 (23.08, 24.87, 23.01), above the paper's Achievement Distillation at 21.79 ± 1.37 over 10 seeds. Plain AD and AD + rarity β = 1 still have one seed each, because an AD run takes 7 hours on the 4 GB laptop.
DEATHS_TEXT:
Every episode in every run ends in death; none reaches Crafter's 10,000-step limit. The median agent lives about 236 steps, and the first night is darkest at step 210. Diamonds need the whole tech tree in one life, so how the agent dies matters as much as what it learns. We replayed the final weights of all 24 runs (4,800 episodes, including the follow-up runs in the sections below) with Crafter's damage code hooked, so every lost health point is attributed to its source.

Zombies cause about half of all deaths, and 69% of those happen at night. The agent is almost always awake when it is killed: it spends only 4% of night-time asleep. Sleeping in the open is dangerous, since a zombie does 7 damage to a sleeping player and 2 to an awake one, out of 9 health. But the agent's answer is to stay up, not to build a shelter. With AD the rarity bonus makes this worse: the share of episodes in which it sleeps at all drops from 85% to 50%, which is why wake up falls in the success-rate table.

The second killer is neglect. In 54% of deaths food, water or energy is at 0. Then health stops regenerating, and a zombie or an arrow finishes the job. Water is the worst: it is empty in 43% of deaths. Skeleton arrows (15–23% of deaths) hit the agent in caves, which is exactly where it has to go for iron and diamonds. Lava takes another 4–8%.

Why it does not plan for any of this: training uses a discount factor γ = 0.95, so the agent effectively looks about 20 steps ahead, while a night lasts about 90. Its network also sees only the current frame, so it cannot remember where it last saw water. The next experiments target these two things.

experiments.title: Longer horizon: γ = 0.99 (negative result)
experiments.html:
The death diagnosis suggested that the agent cannot value surviving the night: γ = 0.95 makes it look only about 20 steps ahead, and a night lasts about 90. We changed only the discount, to γ = 0.99 (a horizon of about 100 steps), and kept everything else as in PPO + rarity β = 2: same code, same bonus, 1M steps, 3 seeds. These runs were trained on a second machine (RTX 5090 laptop, Linux). To check that machine gives the same results, we reran γ = 0.95 seed 0 there. It scored 20.90, against 20.85 on the 4 GB laptop.

γ = 0.99 is worse and does not help survival. The score drops from 20.99 ± 0.87 to 16.94 ± 2.55, and it is lower on every seed (19.8 vs 20.8, 14.9 vs 20.2, 16.1 vs 21.9). The agent dies just as early (median 228 steps vs 230), from the same causes (zombies 55% vs 56% of deaths), and it still sleeps through only about 5% of the night. On two of the three seeds it even falls back behind the stone-pickaxe wall that the rarity bonus had broken (stone pickaxe in 4.8% and 1.6% of episodes, against 17% with γ = 0.95). A longer horizon alone does not teach it to survive the night. Most likely it makes the value targets noisier and the one-off bonus a smaller share of the return, so learning slows down.

One caveat: training uses GAE with λ = 0.65, so the advantage mostly reflects the next few steps whatever γ is. A complete test of a long horizon would also raise λ (for example γ = 0.99, λ = 0.95). The checkpoint videos show a second problem: agents walk right past diamonds. In two of the videos below a diamond is in view, but the agent has no iron pickaxe and dies a few steps later. One of them made a stone sword but never a stone pickaxe, so the iron next to it was out of reach. Remembering where diamonds, iron and water are is the next experiment.

experiments.title: Memory: AD + rarity β = 2 + GRU (negative result)
experiments.html:
Agents walk past diamonds and die of thirst after leaving water behind. The AD network cannot remember either: it sees only the current frame plus the embedding of its last achievement. We added a GRU memory (512 units) between the encoder and the policy and value heads. It is carried from step to step within an episode and reset when a new one starts. PPO trains it with backpropagation through 64-step chunks; AD's contrastive losses are unchanged. γ stays at 0.95 and everything else is the AD + rarity β = 2 configuration: 3 seeds, 1M steps each, about 5.3 hours per run with three in parallel on the RTX 5090 laptop. Before training, a test on real rollouts confirmed that replaying the chunks reproduces the rollout's action probabilities to 1e-5.

Memory lowers the score at 1M steps. The three GRU seeds score 20.91, 21.86 and 18.07 (20.28 ± 1.97). The same configuration without memory scores 23.08, 24.87 and 23.01 (23.65 ± 1.05), so the GRU loses 2.2, 3.0 and 4.9 points seed by seed. It learns more slowly and trails through all of training. At the end its last-100-episode score is 29.9–32.4, against 32.5–34.3 without memory. Survival does not change: median life 234 steps against 242, zombies cause 48% of deaths against 46%, thirst 21% against 18%, and water is empty in 48% of deaths against 45%. Two of the three GRU seeds also sleep much less (they wake up in 47% and 42% of episodes, against 70–74% without memory).

Iron tools stay rare either way. The GRU runs made a few more iron pickaxes: about 6 training episodes across the three seeds against 1, and 3 against 1 in 800 fresh evaluation episodes per configuration. But they made fewer iron swords (1 against 3 in training), and both collect iron equally often (206 and 204 of those 800 episodes). With counts this small that is not a real difference. No run found a diamond. The best GRU episode, below, shows where the agents that get furthest fail. It finishes an iron pickaxe and an iron sword with a diamond four tiles away, then dies one step later of thirst and exhaustion. It had also built three furnaces around itself.

So memory, at least in this form and within 1M steps, is not what holds the agent back. The extra parameters and the recurrent training signal slow learning down. The best agents fail because water, food and energy run out, which points to a survival signal as the next experiment.

experiments.title: Survival signal: AD + rarity β = 2 + vitals shaping (negative result)
experiments.html:
The death diagnosis found food, water or energy at 0 in 54% of deaths, and the agents that get furthest die of exactly that. So we rewarded the agent for keeping its vitals up, with potential-based shaping (Ng, Harada & Russell, 1999). The potential is Φ = Σ over food, water and energy of 1 − ((9 − v)/9)², and the learner gets γ·Φ(next) − Φ(now) on top of the game's reward, with Φ = 0 after death. Topping up a nearly empty vital pays most, letting vitals run down costs a little, and dying costs the comfort the agent had. Shaping of this form provably leaves the optimal policy unchanged. We used α = 1 on top of AD + rarity β = 2, with the same settings and seeds as that baseline: 3 seeds, 1M steps, about 5.1 hours per run with three in parallel. One fix was needed: AD finds achievement moments from the reward (anything above 0.1). The shaping makes drinking when thirsty worth +0.1 without an achievement, so with shaping on, AD reads them from the game's achievement flags instead. That gives exactly upstream's goals on the unshaped reward.

It hits its own target but costs the score. The agents drink more (67, 54 and 60% of training episodes against 54–57%), fewer deaths happen with water at 0 (39% against 45%), and fewer are from thirst (15% against 18%). But they do not live longer: median life is 232 steps against 242, and zombies now cause 52% of deaths against 46%. They also climb the tech tree later (stone pickaxe in 21, 9 and 5% of episodes against 25–31%). In 800 fresh episodes from the two best seeds they made no iron tools at all, against 2 for the baseline and 4 with the GRU in the same test, and they collected iron less often (130 against 204 of 800 episodes). The score falls to 17.80 ± 4.11 (22.26, 16.98, 14.17), against 23.65 ± 1.05, and the seeds spread out much more.

A likely reason is a side effect of this exact form. With γ = 0.95, γΦ(next) − Φ(now) contains a cost of (1 − γ)·Φ, about −0.15, for every step alive, while dying costs about −3. The optimal policy is unchanged in theory. But AD's advantage looks only a few steps ahead (GAE λ = 0.65), so staying alive looks barely better than dying, and two seeds indeed lived shorter lives in training (5,013 and 5,214 episodes in 1M steps, against about 4,600). A cleaner test would use a shaping term without that per-step cost, for example Φ(next) − Φ(now), or reward only refills. The videos also show the agents passing diamonds again, still without an iron pickaxe, and still crafting duplicate tools.

experiments.title: Survival signal without the per-step cost: the first agent that lives longer
experiments.html:
The first survival signal charged about −0.15 for every step alive, from the (1 − γ)·Φ term. This version uses Φ(next) − Φ(now) instead, so a step where nothing changes earns exactly 0. Drinking from empty still pays +0.21 and dying still costs the comfort the agent had. The price is the formal guarantee: under γ = 0.95 this form no longer provably leaves the optimal policy unchanged. Compared with the invariant form, it adds a small (1 − γ)·Φ bonus for being alive and comfortable. Everything else is identical to the first survival runs and to the AD + rarity β = 2 baseline: α = 1, 3 seeds, 1M steps, about 5.2 hours per run.

For the first time, the agent survives longer. Median life in fresh episodes rises from 242 to 266 steps, and the share of agents alive at step 300 from 21.5% to 36.0%. Deaths with water at 0 drop from 45% to 30%, thirst deaths from 18% to 14%, lava from 10% to 4%, and skeleton arrows from 20% to 13%. In training, too, the last 300 episodes last 284 steps against 252. Hunger and fatigue deaths rise from 7% to 20%: agents that live longer have more time for food and energy to run out, and topping those up is harder than finding water. Zombies still cause about half of all deaths (49% against 46%).

The score almost holds. 22.07 ± 1.35 (20.64, 23.32, 22.25) against 23.65 ± 1.05, so it recovers 4.3 of the 5.9 points the first version lost, and the seeds agree again. The tech tree is still a little slower: stone pickaxe in 17–29% of training episodes against 25–31%. These agents collect iron more often than any configuration so far (264 of 800 fresh episodes, against 204 for the baseline and 206 with the GRU), but made no iron tools in that test. An iron pickaxe needs a table and a furnace nearby plus wood and coal, and they rarely put all of that together. The longest life in any of our evaluations, below, is one of these agents: 515 steps, into the second night.

So the per-step cost was the problem with the first version. Without it, the survival signal does what it was meant to, longer lives and fewer thirst deaths, at a small cost in score. That makes it a candidate building block: an agent that survives the night has more time to climb the tree, and the next question is how to turn the extra time into iron tools.

experiments.title: Our own world model, Stage 1: dream vs reality (not ready for Stage 2 yet)
experiments.html:
EMERALD, a world-model agent, makes an iron pickaxe in 41.5% of episodes; our best model-free agent does it in about 0.01%. So we started building our own world model: a network that predicts what the agent will see next, so that later an agent can practise the long crafting chain inside it. Stage 1 trains no agent. It only measures how well the model dreams. The design, with predictions written down before training, is in paper/designs/world_model_stage1.md.

What we built. 3,940 episodes (about 930k frames) recorded from our own agents at different stages of training. A tokenizer turns each 64×64 frame into an 8×8 grid of codes (test PSNR 28.7 dB). A 25.6M-parameter model reads the last 64 steps and predicts the next grid, the next inventory as its own output (our difference from EMERALD), unlocked achievements and death. We trained it twice: on uniformly sampled 64-step windows, and with windows containing an iron, iron-tool or diamond unlock sampled 5× more often (21% of training windows instead of about 5%). The data also hold the only diamond our agents ever mined, shown below.

Results. On 200 dreams from held-out episodes, driven by the real actions, the model beats a “nothing changes” baseline at every horizon. It is good for about 5 steps: 51% of tokens right against 30%, and the materials and tools in the inventory exactly right in 91% of dreams against 54%. By 15 steps it is drifting (items exact 56%), and by 50 it has lost the scene. It predicts crafting almost perfectly one step ahead (table, pickaxes, swords: 95–100% recall). It is weak on everything involving creatures (zombie kills 35% recall, cows 40%), which matches what the tokenizer drops. Night is tracked only loosely (brightness correlation 0.42), and off-screen memory fails: after walking away from water for a median of 14 steps, the dream shows the water again in only 15% of cases (our water detector agrees with the game's own labels in 97%).

Against what we wrote down before training: P1 (≥95% of tokens right 1 step ahead) failed at 74%. P2 (inventory stays right longer than the picture) holds only for materials and tools. P3 (memory within 64 steps) and P4 (night) failed. P5 (rarity weighting helps rare transitions) is not supported: collecting iron was recalled 39% (uniform) against 36% (weighted), the weighting only raised precision (49% → 66%), and there was a single iron-pickaxe event in the test set. The bar for Stage 2, items right in 90% of dreams at 15 steps, is not met (56%). One more weakness: the small inventory and achievement outputs overfit after about 8k of 30k training steps.

So Stage 1 gives a world model that dreams Crafter convincingly for a few steps and knows the crafting rules, but forgets what it cannot see and loses creatures. The next step is either a Stage 1b that fixes those (creature-aware tokens, stopping the small outputs earlier, a training signal for memory), or a Stage 2 that only imagines 5 steps ahead, where the model is already good.
experiments.caption: 200 dreams per model from 392 held-out episodes, each started from a real moment with up to 64 real steps of context and driven by the real actions. “Nothing changes” copies the last real step (for pixels, as the tokenizer draws it). experiments.title: World model Stage 1b: creatures and short dreams fixed, memory not yet
experiments.html:
Stage 1b went after the four Stage 1 failures, one fix each (design and predictions in paper/designs/world_model_stage1b.md). Creatures: a tokenizer whose pixel loss counts each frame's hardest 10% of pixels 5×. Overfitting: after training, the inventory, unlock and death outputs are re-fitted on the frozen model with early stopping on a validation slice. Memory: a skip-ahead output that predicts the frame 4–32 steps later from the actions in between. Drift: a quarter of training windows feed the model its own predictions. Night: an episode-clock input. We also recorded 3,990 more episodes, from new seeds and from agents the first dataset did not use (GRU, both survival signals, γ = 0.99, plain PPO), so the world model trains on 6,753 episodes instead of 3,548. The test set is unchanged: the same 392 held-out episodes and the same 200 dreams as Stage 1.

What worked. The new tokenizer keeps cows, iron ore and most night-time zombies: 19.5 dB on creature tiles against 15.7, and 34.8 dB overall against 28.9. The model now predicts iron collection one step ahead with 92% recall and 93% precision, against 39% and 49%, and eating a cow at 74% against 40%. Dreams hold up longer: the materials and tools are exactly right in 93% of dreams after 5 steps and 62% after 15 (Stage 1: 90.5% and 55.5%). The picture is 1 dB closer to reality at 15 steps on average, though individual dreams can still drift just as fast (the first video below: on the same start, both models lose a lake within 15 steps). Night is tracked better (correlation 0.66 against 0.42), and the re-fitted outputs no longer overfit (test inventory loss 0.028 against 0.054).

What did not. Memory. Water that left the screen comes back in 17% of dreams, against 14.5%, and the ablation without the memory signal also gets 17%. So the skip-ahead output did not carry over into the dreams. Asked directly, it shows the water in 34% of cases. Zombie kills (54% against a target of 60%), dreams at 15 steps (62% against 70%) and night (0.66 against 0.80) improved but stayed below what we wrote down. By the design note's bar, 15-step dreams are not ready. The lower bar, 5-step dreams, is met on accuracy (93%) but not on memory.

Next. Memory is now the main gap, and it is the one the agent needs most: remembering where water, iron or a diamond was. A likely reason it fails is that the agent's own position is never given to the model, so it must infer from the pictures how far it has walked. A Stage 1c could add an explicit map memory: a top-down map the model writes what it sees into, positioned by the moves it makes. Alternatively Stage 2 could start with 5-step dreams, which are already accurate, and leave memory to the agent's own policy.

experiments.title: World model Stage 1c: is memory a matter of knowing where you are?
experiments.html:
After Stage 1b, memory was the main gap: water the agent walked away from came back in only 17% of dreams. One explanation is that the model never knows where the agent is, so it must work out from the pictures how far it walked. We tested that directly. Recording positions was not needed: a move either shifts the 9×7 tile view by one tile or is blocked, and comparing consecutive views settles 98.7% of moves. The reconstructed paths are consistent: a world tile seen again has the same material in 99.9% of 553k revisits. Stage 1c adds the position (relative to the start of each 64-step window) as an input, plus an odometry output that predicts each move, so dreams can keep track of where they walk. It starts from the Stage 1b weights. As a control, Stage 1b was also simply trained twice as long. These positions come from the game's tile map, so Stage 1c is a diagnostic: a real agent would have to estimate its moves from the pictures.

Result: position is not the main bottleneck. With position, water comes back in 21% of dreams and the skip-ahead output finds it in 38%. Twice the training without position gets 23% and 39%. Both are small gains over 17% and 34%, and far from the 50% we would need. Position does make longer dreams a bit more accurate (materials and tools exactly right after 50 steps in 19.5% of dreams, against 15.5%), but its re-fitted outputs predict unlocks less precisely (56% against 73%).

What this points to. The model only keeps one compressed vector per past frame, so redrawing remembered terrain means rebuilding it from a summary. Its 8-pixel tokens also do not line up with Crafter's 7-pixel tiles, so a one-tile move can never be a clean shift of the picture. The next design (paper/designs/world_model_stage1d.md) uses tile-aligned tokens and an explicit top-down map that the model writes what it sees into and reads back when it predicts.

experiments.title: World model Stage 1d: a map the model can read
experiments.html:
Stage 1c showed that knowing the position was not enough. Stage 1d changes two things. First, the picture is cut into Crafter's own tiles: 9×9 tiles of 7×7 pixels, one token each, so a one-tile step is an exact one-token shift. This tile tokenizer is also much sharper (36.2 dB, and 31.8 dB on creatures against 19.5 dB before). Second, the model keeps a top-down map, like a player would. Everything it sees is written at its place in the world, together with when it was seen. Before drawing the next frame, the model reads the part of the map it is about to look at. In a dream it moves by its own predicted steps and writes its own imagined frames into the map. To isolate the map, an identical model without it was trained alongside (30k steps each, about 5.5 hours in parallel).

Result: memory finally works. Water the agent walked away from comes back in 60% of dreams, against 22.5% for the same model without the map and 23% for the best earlier model. That meets the target we wrote down before the run (at least 60%). After 50 steps, 31% of dreams still have exactly the right materials and tools (18% without the map), and 65% of terrain tiles are still right. Night is followed better too (0.73). In the video below, the top row is the map model and the bottom row is the same start without the map: the model without a map fills the stone area with cows that do not exist, while the map model keeps the coal, lava and ground where they were. We had feared the map would leave 'ghost' animals behind where it last saw them. A tile-by-tile grader shows the opposite: the map model draws 0.26 non-existent creatures per frame 50 steps ahead, against 0.65 without the map. One weakness: the unlock outputs are less precise (59% against 70–73%).

Honest positions. The map needs the agent's position, which here came from the game's tile map. We then wrote an odometry that uses pixels only. It compares each frame with the previous one shifted by a tile, learns by itself which tiles can be walked on (for open ground, where both look the same), and recognises sleep from the grey screen. Checked against the game's true position, it is right on 99.8% of steps and keeps the exact position on 99.2% of steps, better than the tile-map path (94%). Maps built from it are as accurate (99.75% of remembered terrain right). The next run (Stage 1e) trains the map model on these pixel positions, and also on its own predictions.
experiments.caption: Same 392 test episodes and 200 dream starts as all earlier stages; re-fitted outputs. Terrain and ghosts: each dreamed tile is classified by a lookup built from real frames (99.5% right on real frames, never reports a creature that is not there). *The 8×8 model draws almost no creatures at all (it finds 14% of real ones one step ahead, against 58% for the map model).

experiments.title: World model Stage 1e: the map from pixels alone
experiments.html:
The Stage 1d map needed the agent's position, which came from the game's tile map. Stage 1e retrains the same model with positions from our pixel-only odometry (right on 99.8% of steps against the game's true position), and a second copy that is also trained on its own predictions for the last 8 steps of a quarter of its training windows.

Result: honest positions cost nothing. Water still comes back in 58.5% of dreams (60% before), and every other measure is the same or slightly better. Using pixel positions only when dreaming, with the Stage 1d model unchanged, also gives exactly 60%. Training on its own predictions changes little: slightly more exact items after 50 steps (33.5% against 32%), slightly less water (56%), but more precise unlock predictions (70% against 59%). So the map memory works without any game internals, which is what lets us give the same kind of map to the playing agent (next section).
experiments.caption: Same 200 dream starts and test set as all earlier stages; re-fitted outputs.

experiments.title: The agent gets its own map (AD + rarity β = 2 + pixel map): it uses it, but the score does not rise
experiments.html:
This tests the idea of memory inside one run directly: remember where the water, the iron or a diamond was. The world-model work showed that a top-down map can be built from pixels alone, so the playing agent now builds one too, from its own frames and actions only, with no game internals. It tracks its position by comparing each frame with the previous one shifted by a tile. It learns while playing which kinds of ground it can walk on (for open ground, where both pictures look the same), and it recognises sleep from the grey screen. Checked against the true position, 99–99.4% of steps are right. Everything it sees is stored at its place in the world. The agent gets an extra 64×64 image: the 32×32 tiles around it (half the world), 2 pixels per tile, never-seen tiles black. A second, smaller image encoder reads it, next to the usual one for the game frame. Everything else is the AD + rarity β = 2 baseline: 3 seeds, 1M steps, about 7.8 hours per run. In the videos, the map is shown to the right of the game, with the agent's tile outlined.

Result: about the same score, a bit longer lives. The score is 22.31 ± 1.00 (21.46, 22.06, 23.42) against 23.65 ± 1.05, within about one standard deviation. In fresh episodes, 27.5% of agents are alive at step 300 against 21.5%, the median life is 248 steps against 242, and zombie deaths while awake drop from 44% to 39%. During training the map agents drink more (62% of episodes against 56%) but collect iron half as often (3.7% against 7.4%).

The agent does read its map. Replaying the final agents on the same 600 fresh worlds with the map blanked out, they unlock 1.3 fewer achievements per episode (12.7 against 14.0), make a stone pickaxe less often (67% against 72%) and live less long (median 237 against 246 steps).

But memory was not what killed it. Thirst deaths rise from 18% to 24%. We checked what the map held in 600 fresh episodes: 282 agents died with water at 0. Only 17 of them had never seen water. In 104 the map held water that the agent had seen but never drunk from, and 161 had drunk earlier and did not go back. The agent has the information; it does not act on it in time. Thirst hurts only slowly and long after the decision that caused it, and with γ = 0.95 the agent barely looks 20 steps ahead. So the next step is not more memory but a reason to use it, for example the no-drift survival signal, which was the one change that cut thirst deaths.

experiments.title: Map + survival signal together: longer lives, lower score
experiments.html:
The map agent had seen water in 95% of its games and still died of thirst, so it lacked a reason to go back in time, not the memory. The no-drift survival signal (a reward for topping up a low vital, α = 1, no per-step cost) was the one change that had cut thirst deaths. Here both are combined on top of AD + rarity β = 2: the map supplies where the water is, the signal why now. Same flags as both parents, 3 seeds, 1M steps. Written down before running: thirst deaths below both parents (under 14%), and a score at least the map agent's 22.31.

Result: both predictions refuted. The score is 20.53 ± 0.46 (20.00, 20.78, 20.81), the lowest of the four, below the map alone (22.31) and the survival signal alone (22.07). Thirst deaths are 17%: fewer than with the map alone (24%), but not fewer than with the signal alone (14%). The agents live as long as with the signal alone (35% alive at step 300, against 21.5% for the baseline) and drink most often (68% of training episodes), but make a stone pickaxe in only 15% of training episodes (baseline 28%) and collect iron in 1.9% (7.4%). More of them die asleep (zombie while asleep 6%, the highest of any configuration).

Reading. Each addition makes the agent safer but slower up the tech tree, and the effects add up: longer lives buy fewer tools, not more. The Crafter score rewards unlocking each achievement once, early, so time spent on vitals is lost. Neither memory nor a survival incentive is what blocks the iron → diamond chain. One training episode (seed 0, at the very end of training) did mine a diamond: 252 steps, 18 achievements, including an iron pickaxe. A single episode, not a trend.

experiments.title: Is the dream an easier world? Zombies and damage in dreams vs reality
experiments.html:
Before an agent practises inside the world model (Stage 2), we need to know whether the dream is as dangerous as Crafter. If it is safer, an agent trained there learns to ignore the night and then dies in the real game. We dreamed 600 times for 50 steps from real moments of held-out episodes, half starting at night, with the real actions. Every dreamed frame was classified tile by tile (the grader from Stage 1d) and compared with what really happened: zombies in view, zombies within reach (next to the player, where Crafter's zombies hit), new zombies walking into view, and how much health the player had lost.

Correction of what we assumed. From the creature recall and precision of Stage 1e we had concluded that creatures fade out of dreams (25–51% as many as in reality). That holds for cows by day, but not for zombies at night: with the map, a greedy dream shows about as many zombies as reality (0.61 per frame at step 50 against 0.51 for real frames through the same grader), and as many within reach.

The dream is easier in a different way: nobody gets hurt. All dreams so far were decoded greedily: every tile takes its single most likely code, and the health counter its most likely value. A hit is never the most likely outcome of one step, so the dreamed player almost never loses health: 0.45 points by step 50 at night against 2.09 in reality, and 0.39 against 1.30 by day. New zombies also almost never walk in from off-screen (5% of dreams against 44%), because on any single tile a zombie appearing is unlikely. A Stage 2 agent trained in these dreams would learn that zombies are harmless.

Sampling fixes the danger, for about 15 steps. Drawing each token and count from the model's own probabilities (temperature 1, as Dreamer-style agents do) gives realistic danger: zombies walk in in 51% of dreams (reality 44%), and health lost by step 50 is 2.37 at night (2.09) and 1.46 by day (1.30). Up to about step 5 everything matches. Beyond that, sampled dreams fill up: by step 50 there are twice the real number of zombies, six times the cows by day, and terrain is right on 54% of tiles instead of 63%. Temperature 0.7 is no compromise: still half the real damage and few walk-ins. The map model is the better base either way; without the map, greedy dreams pile up zombies and skeletons (1.1 zombies per frame at night by step 15, reality 0.26) yet still lose almost no health, so the dreamed health counter is not tied to the zombies drawn.

For Stage 2: dream with sampling, and keep imagination short (5–15 steps, EMERALD and DreamerV3 use 15). There the danger is about right or somewhat higher than in reality, never lower. Greedy dreams must not be used for training: they are the easier world.

Health lost: start health minus health at that step (dream: the model's inventory output). Terrain: share of material tiles whose class is right. † Share of dreams with no zombie in view at the start in which one appears within 50 steps.

experiments.title: Practising in dreams (Stage 2a): the best score so far, but not yet comparable
experiments.html:
Not comparable to the benchmark. This is the diagnostic stage. The world model (v4, frozen) was trained on 6,753 episodes recorded from other agents, so an agent that practises in it has indirectly seen more than its own 1M steps. The honest version, a world model learned only from the agent's own steps, is Stage 2b.

Setup. The best agent (AD + rarity β = 2) plays its 1M real steps exactly as before. In every epoch it also plays 256 short dreams of 16 steps each: each dream starts from a real moment of the last epoch (its 64-step context, inventory and map) and the world model plays the world, sampled at T = 1, which keeps zombies as dangerous as in reality for that long. Half of the starts, and 85% late in training, are frontier moments: the episode has a stone pickaxe but no diamond yet. The reward in the dream is the real one: first unlocks (collect and make read off the dreamed inventory, the rest from the unlock head), 0.1 × health change and the rarity bonus. Dreamed and real steps share every PPO minibatch half and half; AD's goal matching sees real episodes only. Written down before running: collect iron ≥ 15% and iron pickaxe ≥ 0.5% of training episodes (P15), a score of at least 22.6 (P16), the dream never paying much more than reality (P17), and no more deaths (P18).

Result: the best score so far, 26.10 ± 0.75 (25.62, 25.73, 26.96), against 23.65 ± 1.05 for the same agent without dreams; every dream seed is above the best baseline seed. The gain is in the iron chain: furnace 47% (37%), stone pickaxe 38.5% (28%), collect iron 15.4% (7.4%), iron sword 0.18% (0.02%), iron pickaxe 0.09% (0.01%). Still no diamond. With the final weights, 2,400 fresh episodes (800 per seed) reach iron in 46% and make 8 iron pickaxes (the GRU agent: 3 in 1,600), and again no diamond. 7 of those 8 die of an empty vital. P15 is half met (iron yes, iron pickaxe no), P16 and P17 hold: the dream paid iron at 1.2–1.3× the real rate and every other achievement below it, so there was nothing fake to exploit.

What it cost: sleep. Wake up falls from 72% to 44% of training episodes. In the death diagnosis more agents are alive at step 300 (28.7%, baseline 21.5%) and fewer are killed by zombies while awake (36%, 44%), but more die of thirst (25%, 18%) and while asleep (8%, 2%), often by day, in a cave, with no water. The likely cause is the dream itself: it pays waking up at a third of the real rate, and a 16-step dream cannot show what sleeping in a bad place costs 50 steps later.

What the dream did not do. In about 3M dreamed steps per seed the dream never paid an iron sword, an iron pickaxe or a diamond. Dreams taught the way to iron; the few iron tools came from real play building on it. Two checks come before Stage 2b: whether the world model can dream the iron-pickaxe craft at all from a real moment just before one, and paying wake up and drink at their real rates in dreams.

experiments.title: Can the world model dream an iron pickaxe? No: it has seen four
experiments.html:
Stage 2a's dreams never paid an iron tool or a diamond. Is that the agent not trying in the dream, or the world model not knowing the craft? To separate the two, the policy is taken out: dreams start from real moments 1 to 16 steps before a real craft, replay the real actions, and we check whether the dreamed inventory shows the item by the step it really appeared (+2 steps). Same dreaming as in Stage 2a (64-step context, map, T = 1, 32 dreams per moment). The moments come from 9,000 fresh episodes of the Stage 2a agents, recorded separately so that no world model trained on them, and tokenized and positioned online exactly as in training.

Result: the world model cannot make an iron tool. The common steps are dreamed 56–99% of the time, but of 41 iron-pickaxe and 47 iron-sword crafts not one appears in any of the 11,264 dreams (2,816 per start distance); on average the inventory output gives the new tool a probability below 1%. In the dream the agent stands at the table and furnace with wood, coal and iron, presses the craft action, and nothing happens. On its own training episodes it does recall 2 of its 4 iron-pickaxe crafts, so it memorised those, without learning the rule.

Why. The data: the 7,134 episodes it learned from (1.76M steps of other agents) contain 2,440 iron pickups and 4,726 stone pickaxes, but 4 iron pickaxes, no iron sword and 1 diamond. A world model trained on the agent's own 1M steps (Stage 2b) would have even fewer: 0–1 iron pickaxes from the plain agent, 3–5 from the dreaming one. As built, Stage 2b would hit the same ceiling. What would lift it is a world model that can generalise a craft it has hardly seen from the many it has: crafting is the same rule for every tool (an action next to a table, some items go down, one goes up), and our inventory output currently learns each item's count separately.
experiments.caption: Share of dreams (32 per moment, sampled at T = 1, real actions) whose inventory shows the item by the step it really appeared (+2), started 1, 4, 8 or 16 steps before. Controls are 100 random moments per item from the same episodes.

videos.title: Real craft vs dream (held-out episode)
videos.desc: The dream starts 7 steps before a real iron-pickaxe craft and follows the same actions. Terrain, table and furnace stay right; at the craft step reality spends wood, coal and iron for the pickaxe (blue), while the dream's inventory does not change (red).

experiments.title: A shared craft rule: the world model now dreams iron tools (Stage 2a rerun running)
experiments.html:
The world model learned each item's count on its own, so 4 iron pickaxes in 1.76M steps taught it nothing. Yet the rule is the same for every tool: press a craft action with certain items at hand and a station within reach, the items are used up and the tool count goes up by one. We added a small craft layer with exactly that shape, learned from the same data on the frozen world model. It is a learned AND over item thresholds and stations in reach, plus a fixed effect. Pickaxe and sword of the same material share one recipe; this is the one piece of prior knowledge put in by us.

What is learned, and from what.

  • Which tiles are a table or a furnace comes from the agent's own placing. When a table is placed and one neighbouring tile changes, that tile is tracked at its world position for the rest of the episode, by night too. Result: 14 table and 11 furnace codes that find 99.7% / 98.8% of real stations in reach, with no false detections. The simulator's labels were used only to check this.
  • What a craft uses up must be at hand. This is needed because the data cannot show that iron tools need coal: no iron press ever failed with only coal missing.
  • An "awake" term, read from the world model's view of the current frame. It is needed because 1,700 presses with everything at hand failed while the player was asleep.
  • The HUD is redrawn from the dreamed inventory, so the agent sees the tool it made.

Result.

  • The learned recipes match Crafter's for all 6 tools, iron sword included, which has no example at all.
  • On the same held-out crafts as above, the dream now shows the iron pickaxe 97% and the iron sword 99% of the time one step ahead, where v4 alone showed 0%.
  • False crafts: 0.012 per 10,000 presses that miss a requirement.
  • Over 16 dreamed steps the rate falls to 63–69%, the same drift as the controls.
  • Diamonds are still not dreamed: mining is a different rule, with 1 example.

The Stage 2a rerun with the layer (3 seeds, 1M steps, still not 1M-comparable) started on 30 Oct. The prediction: iron pickaxe and iron sword in at least 0.5% of training episodes, without the score falling.
